Priority ceilings also help prevent some deadlocks

title: Thread Pools: Sizing, Queues and Rejection
objectives: Size a pool from cores and the share of time tasks spend waiting
Bound the queue and choose what happens when it is full
Avoid deadlocks where tasks wait on the pool they run in

cards.title: Why pools exist
cards.body: Creating a thread costs memory for its stack and a trip through the kernel, and thousands of threads compete for a few cores. A pool keeps a fixed set of worker threads that take tasks from a queue. Three numbers define it: how many workers, how long the queue may grow, and what happens to a task that arrives when both are full.

cards.title: Worked example: sizing from wait time
cards.body: A service on 8 cores (illustrative numbers).
steps: Each task computes for 10 ms and waits 40 ms on a database
A worker keeps a core busy only 10 ÷ 50 = 20% of the time
To keep 8 cores busy: 8 × (1 + 40 ÷ 10) = 40 workers
At full use the pool finishes at most 8 cores ÷ 10 ms = 800 tasks a second; how many workers a given arrival rate needs is a separate question, answered by Little’s Law
More workers than this cannot add CPU; they only queue on the database

cards.title: Trap: one slow dependency takes every worker
cards.body: If one downstream service slows from 20 ms to 2 s, every task that calls it holds a worker a hundred times longer, and soon all workers are waiting on it. Requests that never touch that service now queue behind them too. Give each blocking dependency its own small pool or a concurrency limit (a bulkhead), and set timeouts shorter than the caller’s deadline so a stuck call frees its worker.

cards.title: Misconception: one big pool is simplest
cards.body: If a task running in a pool submits a sub-task to the same pool and waits for it, every worker can end up waiting for sub-tasks that have no free worker to run them: a deadlock. Run sub-tasks on a separate pool, or have the waiting task run them itself, and never block a worker on the pool it belongs to.

cards.title: Watching a pool
cards.body: Four measurements show a pool’s health: active workers, queue length, time tasks spend queued, and rejections. Queue time rising while workers are all busy means the pool or its downstream is saturated; workers idle while the queue grows means tasks are stuck waiting on something. Alert on queue time, which is what callers feel, rather than on thread count.

questions.prompt: A CPU-bound image resizer runs on a 16-core machine and never waits on I/O. About how many pool workers should it start with?

choices.label: About 16, one per core
About 160, so that tasks do not queue
About 4, to leave cores free for the kernel
One per pending request, created on demand

questions.explanation: Tasks that never wait can keep at most one core busy each, so about one worker per core uses the machine fully. More workers add switching and cache misses without more CPU, a quarter of the cores wastes capacity, and one thread per request is the unbounded model a pool exists to avoid.

questions.prompt: Under a traffic spike, a service’s latency climbs from 50 ms to 40 s and memory keeps growing, but it returns no errors. What is the most likely design flaw?

choices.label: The pool has too few workers for normal traffic
Tasks queue without limit instead of being rejected
The garbage collector is tuned for throughput
Workers are pinned to specific cores

questions.explanation: Growing latency and memory with no errors is the signature of an unbounded queue absorbing overload. Too few workers would also show at normal load, collector tuning does not explain 40 s waits with steady growth, and pinning affects cache behaviour, not queueing.

questions.prompt: A report task runs in a 10-worker pool, submits 3 sub-tasks to the same pool and waits for them. With 10 reports in flight, everything stops. Why?

choices.label: Sub-tasks are run in reverse order of submission
The pool’s queue is too short to hold 30 sub-tasks
All 10 workers wait on sub-tasks no worker is free to run
Waiting on a future is not allowed inside a pool

questions.explanation: Every worker holds a report that waits on queued sub-tasks, and no worker is free to run them, so nothing progresses. Ordering does not matter, a longer queue still leaves the sub-tasks unrun, and waiting is allowed; it is waiting on your own pool that deadlocks.

questions.prompt: A batch importer submits work to a pool far faster than the pool finishes it. Which overflow policy fits best?
constraints: The importer can slow down without harm

approaches.label: Run overflow on the submitting thread
approaches.description: When the queue is full, the importer executes the task itself, which slows its submissions.

approaches.label: Reject overflow with an error
approaches.description: The pool throws away work it cannot queue and reports a failure.

approaches.label: Use an unbounded queue
approaches.description: Accept everything and let the queue grow.

rationaleOptions.label: It applies backpressure, so the producer slows to the pool’s pace
It keeps memory bounded because the queue never grows past its limit
It guarantees the fastest possible completion of each record
It removes the need to size the pool at all

questions.explanation: Caller-runs turns overflow into backpressure: the importer does the work itself and submits more slowly, nothing is dropped, and the queue stays bounded. Rejecting would lose records unless the importer retried, and an unbounded queue breaks the memory limit. It does not make each record faster, and the pool still needs a size.

questions.prompt: A service runs on 4 cores. Each task computes for 5 ms and then waits 45 ms on remote calls. How many workers keep all 4 cores busy?
assumptions: Waiting uses no CPU
Enough tasks are always queued
questions.explanation: Design implication: the remote service must handle 40 concurrent calls from this one instance; if it cannot, more workers just move the queue downstream.

questions.prompt: Put in order the checks a typical pool makes for a newly submitted task as load rises.

items.label: Otherwise start an extra worker if below the maximum
Give it to an idle worker if one exists
Otherwise apply the overflow policy
Otherwise place it in the queue if there is room

questions.explanation: Idle worker, then queue, then grow, then reject or push back. Note that with an unbounded queue the last two steps never happen.

flashcards.back: Cores × (1 + wait time ÷ compute time).
When the queue is full, the submitting thread runs the task itself, so producers slow to the pool’s pace.
Tasks wait on sub-tasks queued to the same pool with no free worker to run them.

mechanism.title: How a pool handles a task
steps: A submitted task first goes to an idle worker if there is one, or a new worker is started while the pool is below its core size.
If all core workers are busy, the task waits in the queue. A bounded queue has a capacity; an unbounded one accepts everything.
Some pools start extra workers, up to a maximum, only when the queue is full; with an unbounded queue that never happens, so the maximum has no effect.
When the queue is full and the pool is at its maximum, the overflow policy runs: reject with an error, run on the caller, or discard a task.
Workers loop: take a task, run it, repeat. Extra workers above the core size exit after an idle timeout.

Throughput is capped by the lowest of workers ÷ task time, available cores, and what downstream services can take. How queue time grows as load nears that cap is queueing maths (Little’s Law and utilisation) rather than pool mechanics.

useWhen: Use separate bounded pools for work with different dependencies.
Use caller-runs or rejection to push overload back to producers.
avoidWhen: Avoid unbounded queues on request paths.
Avoid blocking a pool’s worker on tasks submitted to the same pool.

numbers.title: What the queue bound decides in an overload
assumptions: 40 workers, each task 40 ms, so the pool finishes 1,000 tasks a second
A spike brings 1,250 tasks a second for 60 s
Callers time out at 300 ms; a queued task holds about 20 KB (illustrative)
steps: Excess: 1,250 − 1,000 = 250 tasks a second more than the pool can finish.
Unbounded queue: after 60 s it holds 250 × 60 = 15,000 tasks, about 15,000 × 20 KB = 300 MB, and a new task waits 15,000 ÷ 1,000 = 15 s, so every caller has given up long before its task runs.

Queue bounded at 200 with rejection: a queued task waits at most 200 ÷ 1,000 = 0.2 s, plus 40 ms to run, so 240 ms, inside the timeout; the excess 250 a second, 20% of arrivals, fail at once and can back off.
Caller-runs instead of rejection: the submitting threads run the excess themselves, so producers slow to what the system finishes and nothing is dropped, at the cost of slower submitters.
numbers.result: The bound turns a minute of overload from 300 MB of stale work that nobody receives into fast, visible rejections for 20% of tasks; caller-runs is the alternative when producers can wait.

india.title: What a standard pool’s documentation warns
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The documentation for one widely used standard library thread pool explains that using an unbounded queue causes new tasks to wait when all core threads are busy, so no more than the core number of threads is ever created and the maximum pool size has no effect. It notes that this allows unbounded growth of the queue when tasks arrive faster than they are processed, that the default handler rejects overflow with an error, and that the caller-runs policy provides a simple feedback mechanism that slows the rate at which new tasks are submitted.

pitfalls.trap: “Make the pool bigger until latency drops.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d check whether workers are waiting downstream; if so, more workers only move the queue there.”

pitfalls.trap: “An unbounded queue means we never drop requests.”
pitfalls.say: “It means we answer them after the caller has timed out; I’d bound it and reject early.”

takeaways: Size pools from cores and the wait-to-compute ratio.
Bound the queue to what fits in the caller’s deadline.
Choose an overflow policy deliberately; caller-runs gives backpressure.
Never block a worker on its own pool.

interactive.title: What does doubling the pool do?
interactive.prompt: A pool of 50 workers is saturated; every task spends most of its time waiting on a database that already runs at 100% CPU. Someone doubles the pool to 100.

choices.label: Throughput stays about the same and database latency rises
choices.feedback: Right: the database is the bottleneck, so more concurrent calls only lengthen its queue.

choices.label: Throughput roughly doubles because twice as many tasks run
choices.feedback: Twice as many tasks wait, but the database finishes queries no faster.

choices.label: Throughput falls to zero as the pool deadlocks
choices.feedback: Nothing here waits on its own pool, so there is no deadlock.

interactive.reveal: Pool size only helps while the pool itself is the bottleneck. Find the saturated resource first; here it is the database, so reduce or cache its queries, or limit concurrency to what it can serve.

seeAlso.why: Concurrency models that pools implement
Every extra worker adds context switches
Bounded queues and semaphores that pools are built from
Connection pools: the same bound, queue and reject mechanics for database connections
Little’s Law and utilisation: the queueing maths behind pool and queue sizes

title: Page Replacement, Swapping and Thrashing
objectives: Explain how the kernel chooses which pages to evict when memory runs short
Estimate how a small fault rate slows every memory access
Recognise thrashing and tell swap activity from swap usage

cards.title: Two kinds of pages to evict
cards.body: When free memory runs low, the kernel reclaims pages. Clean file pages, such as program code or cached file data, can simply be dropped and read back from the file later. Dirty file pages must be written back first. Anonymous pages, such as heap and stack, have no file behind them, so they can be evicted only if there is swap space to write them to.

cards.title: Approximating least recently used
cards.body: Evicting the page used longest ago would be ideal but tracking exact order on every access is too costly. Hardware sets an accessed bit when a page is touched; the kernel periodically scans and clears these bits, keeping pages seen again on an active list and moving the rest to an inactive list, from which it evicts. This clock-like scheme keeps recently used pages in memory at low cost.

cards.title: Worked example: one fault in ten thousand
cards.body: Average access time when some accesses fault to disk (illustrative).
steps: A memory access takes 100 ns
A fault that reads a page from a hard disk takes 10 ms, which is 10,000,000 ns
With one fault per 10,000 accesses: 100 + 10,000,000 ÷ 10,000 = 1,100 ns
The average access is 11 times slower, from a fault rate of only 0.01%
With a solid-state disk at 100 µs per fault, the same rate costs 100 + 10 = 110 ns

cards.title: Trap: turning off swap does not stop thrashing
cards.body: Without swap, anonymous pages cannot be evicted, so under pressure the kernel evicts what it still can: file pages, including the code of running programs. Programs then fault their own instructions back in from disk over and over, and the machine thrashes anyway, or the out-of-memory killer ends a process. Swap is not the cause of thrashing; a working set larger than memory is.

cards.title: Misconception: swap in use means memory is short
cards.body: Pages swapped out long ago and never touched again can sit in swap indefinitely, freeing memory for useful cache. What matters is the rate of pages moving in and out per second, and how long tasks stall waiting for memory, which Linux reports as memory pressure stall information. High swap usage with near-zero swap-in is fine; steady swap-in under load is the warning sign.

questions.prompt: Memory is short and the machine has no swap. Which pages can the kernel still reclaim?

choices.label: Heap pages of idle processes, which are written to a temporary file
Only pages belonging to the process using the most memory
File-backed pages, such as cached data and program code
None, so it ends a process straight away

questions.explanation: File-backed pages can be dropped and re-read from their files, after writing back any that are dirty. Anonymous heap pages need swap, and the kernel does not invent a temporary file for them. Reclaim spans all processes rather than the largest one, and the out-of-memory killer runs only after reclaim fails.

questions.prompt: A server shows 6 GB of swap in use, swap-in near zero and steady response times. What should you conclude?

choices.label: Memory is short; add RAM before it gets worse
Rarely used pages were swapped out and are staying there
Swap is broken, because used swap should be read back
The page cache has been disabled by the kernel

questions.explanation: Pages that are never touched again stay in swap harmlessly; the low swap-in rate and steady latency show no pressure. Usage alone does not show a shortage, nothing requires swapped pages to return, and the page cache is unaffected.

questions.prompt: Under load, a host’s CPU is mostly idle, disk reads are at maximum, and every request is slow. Memory pressure stall figures are high. What is happening?

choices.label: The working set no longer fits, so pages keep faulting in
The CPU is overheating and throttling its clock speed
The disk is failing and retrying each read several times
Too many threads are spinning on locks in user space

questions.explanation: Idle CPU, saturated reads and high memory stalls together mean processes spend their time waiting for pages that were evicted and are needed again: thrashing. Throttling would show busy CPUs running slowly, a failing disk would not raise memory stall time, and spinning threads would make the CPU busy, not idle.

questions.prompt: A host thrashes after a new service is added. Which fix addresses the cause?

choices.label: Disable swap so that nothing can be paged out
Raise each process’s scheduling priority
Add more swap space on a faster disk
Cut memory use or move a service elsewhere

questions.explanation: Thrashing means the combined working sets exceed RAM, so reduce demand or add memory. Disabling swap shifts eviction to program code and invites the out-of-memory killer, priorities do not make memory larger, and more swap gives more room to page into without reducing the paging.

questions.prompt: A memory access takes 100 ns. One in every 10,000 accesses faults and waits 10 ms for a disk read. What is the average time per access in nanoseconds?
assumptions: Faults are spread evenly across accesses
Non-faulting accesses all take 100 ns
questions.formula: access time + fault cost × fault rate
questions.explanation: Sanity check: a 0.01% fault rate makes memory 11 times slower here, which is why even light paging is so visible; to stay within 10% of normal speed the fault rate must be below one in a million.

questions.prompt: Order what happens to an anonymous page that stops being used on a host under memory pressure, until it is evicted.

items.label: It moves to the inactive list
Its contents are written to swap and its frame is freed
The reclaim scan finds its accessed bit clear
It is still not touched before the next scan

questions.explanation: Pages earn eviction by staying untouched across scans; a touch in between would move it back to the active list.

flashcards.front: Which pages need swap to be evicted?
flashcards.back: Anonymous pages, such as heap and stack; file pages can be dropped and re-read.
Working sets exceed RAM, so pages are evicted and faulted back in constantly.
Usage is harmless by itself; sustained swap-in and memory stalls signal pressure.

sources.title: Concepts overview, Linux memory management (kernel documentation)

mechanism.title: How the kernel reclaims memory
steps: Each zone of memory has watermarks. When free pages fall below the low mark, a background reclaim thread wakes and frees pages until the high mark is reached.
Pages sit on active and inactive lists, separately for file and anonymous memory. Reclaim scans inactive pages; a page whose accessed bit was set gets another chance on the active list.

Clean file pages are dropped, dirty ones are written back first, and anonymous pages are written to swap if it exists. A swappiness setting tilts the balance between reclaiming file pages and swapping anonymous ones.
If background reclaim cannot keep up, an allocating process reclaims directly and stalls; this direct reclaim is where latency appears.
A page evicted and then needed again causes a major fault: the process blocks while the page is read back. When most faults are refaults of recently evicted pages, the system is thrashing.

If reclaim fails, the out-of-memory killer picks a process to end, preferring those using the most memory adjusted by a per-process score. Containers add a second layer: each memory control group has its own limit and reclaims, and kills, within itself before the whole host is short.

useWhen: Use swap as a buffer for cold anonymous pages, so RAM holds hot data and cache.
Use memory pressure stall figures to alert on real contention.
avoidWhen: Avoid running working sets close to or above RAM.
Avoid treating swap usage, rather than swap-in rate, as an alarm.

rows: Low, with tasks waiting on I/O

numbers.title: How much paging a service can afford
assumptions: Memory access 100 ns; each fault reads from a solid-state disk in 100 µs; acceptable slowdown 10% (illustrative)
steps: Allowed extra time per access: 10% of 100 ns = 10 ns.
Fault cost: 100 µs = 100,000 ns.
Maximum fault rate: 10 ÷ 100,000 = one fault per 10,000 accesses.
On a hard disk at 10 ms per fault the limit becomes 10 ÷ 10,000,000, one per million accesses, a hundred times stricter.
numbers.result: Even a fast disk allows only about one fault per 10,000 accesses before memory feels 10% slower, so paging must stay rare for hot data.

india.title: What the kernel documentation says about reclaim
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The Linux memory management concepts guide explains that pages backed by files can be freed after writing any changes back, while anonymous pages can be reclaimed only by writing them to a swap area. It describes how, when memory runs low, the kernel frees pages by reclaim, and if the system cannot free enough, the out-of-memory killer chooses a task to end. The kernel’s pressure stall documentation adds that memory pressure figures report the share of time tasks are stalled waiting for memory.

pitfalls.trap: “Swap is full, so we need more RAM.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d check swap-in rate and memory stall time; cold pages in swap are harmless.”

pitfalls.trap: “Disable swap to avoid thrashing.”
pitfalls.say: “Thrashing comes from working sets bigger than RAM; without swap the kernel evicts program code instead.”

takeaways: File pages can be dropped; anonymous pages need swap.
A tiny fault rate can multiply average access time.
Watch swap-in rate and stall time, not swap usage.
Fix thrashing by cutting demand or adding memory.

interactive.title: What happens without swap?
interactive.prompt: A host has no swap. Its processes’ heaps grow until free memory is nearly gone, and they keep growing slowly.

choices.label: The kernel evicts program code and cache, then kills a process
choices.feedback: Right: only file pages can go, so programs refault their own code, and finally the out-of-memory killer acts.

choices.label: The heaps stop growing because allocation fails at once
choices.feedback: Most allocations succeed until reclaim runs out of options; failure is not immediate.

choices.label: Nothing changes until memory is completely full, then it slows
choices.feedback: Reclaim starts at the low watermark, well before memory is full.

interactive.reveal: Without swap, heap pages are pinned in RAM, so all reclaim pressure lands on file pages, including executable code. Latency degrades before the out-of-memory killer finally ends a process.

seeAlso.why: Page tables and faults that reclaim relies on
The page cache is the main pool of reclaimable file pages
Huge pages change how memory is mapped and reclaimed

title: The TLB and Huge Pages
objectives: Explain what the translation lookaside buffer caches and why misses are costly
Calculate TLB reach for different page sizes
Decide when huge pages help and when transparent ones hurt

cards.title: A cache for address translations
cards.body: Every memory access needs its virtual address translated to a physical one, which would mean walking several levels of page tables each time. The translation lookaside buffer (TLB) is a small hardware cache of recent translations. A hit costs almost nothing; a miss makes the hardware walk the tables, adding several memory accesses, each of which may miss the data caches too.

cards.title: Worked example: TLB reach
cards.body: How much memory a TLB can cover (illustrative entry count).
steps: Suppose the second-level TLB holds 1,536 entries
With 4 KiB pages, reach = 1,536 × 4 KiB = 6 MiB
A 2 GiB hash table accessed at random misses the TLB on almost every lookup
With 2 MiB pages, reach = 1,536 × 2 MiB = 3 GiB, which covers the whole table
Each 2 MiB page also replaces 512 page table entries, so walks that do happen are shorter

cards.title: Explicit and transparent huge pages
cards.body: Huge pages can be reserved explicitly at boot or at run time and mapped by programs that ask for them; they are never swapped and are guaranteed to exist. Transparent huge pages let the kernel use 2 MiB pages for ordinary memory automatically, either everywhere or only where a program advises it, and a background thread merges small pages into huge ones when it can.

cards.title: Trap: transparent huge pages and latency spikes
cards.body: To create a huge page the kernel needs 2 MiB of contiguous free memory. When memory is fragmented it may stop an allocating thread to compact memory, causing pauses, and a program that touches one byte of a region can be given the whole 2 MiB, bloating memory use. Systems with many small, scattered allocations often run better with transparent huge pages limited to programs that request them.

cards.title: Misconception: huge pages make memory faster
cards.body: Huge pages do not make RAM or the data caches faster; they make translation cheaper. A program whose working set already fits in TLB reach, or that streams memory sequentially, sees little change. The gains come for large working sets accessed at random, such as big hash tables, in-memory databases and virtual machines, where page walks are a measurable share of time.

questions.prompt: What does the TLB store?

choices.label: Recently used data lines copied from main memory
Recent virtual-to-physical address translations
The list of pages waiting to be written to swap
Each thread’s registers saved at a context switch

questions.explanation: The TLB caches translations so most accesses skip the page table walk. Data lines live in the data caches, swap candidates are kernel lists in ordinary memory, and saved registers are kept in kernel memory for each thread.

questions.prompt: Which workload is most likely to speed up noticeably with 2 MiB pages?

choices.label: A tool that reads a 50 GB log file once from start to end
A web handler that touches 200 KB of memory per request
A 20 GiB in-memory index probed at random keys
A program that sleeps on network input most of the time

questions.explanation: Random probes across 20 GiB miss a 4 KiB-page TLB constantly, and larger pages raise reach enough to cut those misses. Sequential reads are dominated by disk and prefetching, a 200 KB footprint already fits in TLB reach, and a mostly sleeping program has no translation bottleneck.

questions.prompt: After transparent huge pages were set to apply everywhere, a cache server shows occasional 100 ms pauses and higher memory use. What is the likely cause?

choices.label: The kernel compacts memory to build huge pages and fills sparse regions
Huge pages are written to swap more often than small pages
The TLB is flushed each time a huge page is created
Huge pages make each cache line 2 MiB long

questions.explanation: Building 2 MiB pages can force compaction stalls when memory is fragmented, and sparsely used regions get whole huge pages, raising memory use. Transparent huge pages are usually split before swapping rather than swapped more, creating one does not flush the whole TLB, and cache line size is fixed by hardware.

questions.prompt: Why does switching between two processes typically cost more in TLB terms than switching between two threads of one process?

choices.label: Threads of one process use physical addresses directly
Processes have different address spaces, so translations differ
Process switches also flush the data caches
The TLB stores entries only for the kernel’s own threads

questions.explanation: Threads share one address space, so their TLB entries stay valid; another process has different translations, so entries must be flushed or tagged by address-space ID, and the new process starts with fewer hits. Threads do use virtual addresses, data caches are not flushed on a normal switch, and the TLB holds user translations too.

questions.prompt: A lookup service makes 20 million random probes a second. 40% of them miss the TLB, and each miss costs about 25 ns of page walking. How many milliseconds of core time per second go to page walks?
assumptions: Miss cost does not overlap with other work
Every probe is a single memory access
questions.formula: probes × miss rate × cost per miss
questions.explanation: Design implication: a fifth of a core goes to translation alone; if huge pages cut the miss rate to 4%, that falls to 20 ms, so measuring the miss rate tells you whether huge pages are worth their risks.

questions.prompt: Order what happens on a load instruction whose translation is not in the TLB, until the data arrives.

items.label: The physical address is used to fetch the data
The hardware walks the page table levels in memory
The TLB lookup misses
The translation is installed in the TLB

questions.explanation: Miss, walk, install, access. A fault is raised only if the walk finds no valid entry, which is the page fault case.

flashcards.back: A small hardware cache of virtual-to-physical translations.
Entries × page size; 1,536 entries cover 6 MiB with 4 KiB pages or 3 GiB with 2 MiB pages.
Compaction stalls and memory bloat from sparsely used 2 MiB regions.

mechanism.title: What a TLB miss costs
steps: A load or store presents a virtual address. The core checks a small first-level TLB, then a larger second-level one, in parallel with starting the cache lookup.
On a miss, a hardware page walker reads the page table levels, four on common 64-bit systems, starting from the root held in a register; upper levels are often in the data caches.
If the final entry is valid, the translation is installed in the TLB and the access proceeds. If it is not, a page fault is raised and the kernel takes over.
With a 2 MiB page, the walk stops one level early and one entry covers 512 times as much memory, so both the miss rate and the cost of each miss fall.

Changing address space, as on a switch between processes, invalidates entries unless they are tagged with an address-space identifier; changing a mapping requires shooting down stale entries on other cores, which costs an interrupt to each.
Transparent huge pages are created at fault time when an aligned 2 MiB region is free, or later by a background thread that collapses small pages; failing that, ordinary 4 KiB pages are used.

useWhen: Use huge pages for large, randomly accessed, long-lived memory such as database buffer pools and virtual machine memory.
Use advise-only transparent mode so programs opt in.
avoidWhen: Avoid enabling transparent huge pages everywhere for sparse, fragmented allocation patterns.
Avoid expecting gains for small or sequential working sets.

rows: 1.5 TiB in theory; real CPUs hold far fewer 1 GiB entries

numbers.title: Is translation worth fixing?
assumptions: A lookup service misses the TLB on 30% of 50 million probes a second; each miss costs about 30 ns of page walking (illustrative)
steps: Walking time: 15,000,000 × 30 ns = 0.45 s of core time per second.
With huge pages covering the table, suppose misses drop to 3%: 1,500,000 × 30 ns = 0.045 s.
Saving: about 0.4 core-seconds per second, nearly half a core freed.
numbers.result: Here huge pages free almost half a core, worth doing; at a 1% miss rate the same change would save under 0.02 cores and not be worth the risks.

india.title: What the kernel documentation says huge pages buy
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The kernel’s memory concepts guide explains that the TLB is usually a scarce resource, and applications with large memory working sets suffer a performance hit because of TLB misses; mapping 2 MiB or 1 GiB pages significantly reduces pressure on the TLB and improves its hit rate. The transparent huge page guide adds that a huge page reduces page faults by a factor of 512 for the region it covers and makes TLB misses run faster, but warns that the kernel may need to compact memory to find contiguous space.

pitfalls.trap: “Turn on huge pages everywhere for speed.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d measure TLB miss rates first and opt in only large, random-access memory.”

pitfalls.trap: “The pauses must be garbage collection.”
pitfalls.say: “They could be compaction for transparent huge pages; I’d check kernel stall counters too.”

takeaways: The TLB caches translations; misses walk the page tables.
Reach equals entries times page size.
Huge pages help large random-access working sets.
Transparent huge pages can cause compaction pauses and bloat.

interactive.title: Will huge pages help this job?
interactive.prompt: A batch job scans a 100 GB file sequentially, once, processing each record as it goes. Someone proposes enabling huge pages to speed it up.

choices.label: Little change: sequential scanning has few TLB misses per byte
choices.feedback: Right: each 4 KiB page serves 4,096 consecutive bytes, so translation is a tiny share of the work.

choices.label: A large speedup, because 100 GB is far beyond TLB reach
choices.feedback: Size alone does not matter; the access pattern does, and sequential access misses rarely.

choices.label: It will fail, since huge pages cannot hold file data
choices.feedback: Whether file data can use huge pages depends on the file system, but either way the gain here is small.

interactive.reveal: Huge pages pay off when accesses jump around a large working set. A one-pass sequential scan is limited by disk or memory bandwidth, not by translations.

seeAlso.why: Page tables are what the TLB caches
Data caches and locality, the other half of memory speed
Reclaim and compaction interact with huge pages

title: Inter-Process Communication: Pipes, Sockets and Shared Memory
objectives: Choose between pipes, local sockets and shared memory for passing data between processes
Use a full pipe buffer as backpressure, and avoid the deadlock it can cause
Weigh copy and system-call costs against the synchronisation shared memory needs

cards.title: Three ways to talk
cards.body: A pipe is a one-way byte stream held in a kernel buffer: one process writes, another reads. A local (Unix domain) socket is two-way, can carry separate messages as well as streams, and can pass open file descriptors and the sender’s identity. Shared memory maps the same physical pages into both processes, so data is not copied by the kernel at all, but the processes must coordinate access themselves.

cards.title: A full buffer is backpressure
cards.body: A pipe’s buffer is limited, 64 KiB by default on Linux. When it is full, a writer blocks until the reader drains some of it, so a fast producer is slowed to the consumer’s pace without any extra code. Writes no larger than a small atomic limit, 4 KiB on Linux, are never interleaved with other writers’ data, which makes a pipe safe for several writers of short records.

cards.title: Trap: the two-pipe deadlock
cards.body: A parent feeds a child through one pipe and reads its output through another.
steps: The parent writes 1 MB of input to the child’s input pipe before reading anything
The child reads input and writes results to its output pipe as it goes
The output pipe fills at 64 KiB, so the child blocks on its write and stops reading input
The input pipe then fills, so the parent blocks on its write
Each waits for the other. Fix: read output while writing input, using a second thread or readiness polling

cards.title: Misconception: shared memory is the fast choice for everything
cards.body: Shared memory removes copies, but the reader still has to learn that new data has arrived, either by polling, which burns a core, or by sleeping on a futex or semaphore, which costs system calls much like a socket. It also needs careful memory ordering and offers no protection if one side corrupts the region. For messages of a few kilobytes, a local socket’s copy is cheap; shared memory pays off for large or very frequent transfers.

cards.title: Worked example: what a message costs
cards.body: Sending a 1 KB message over a local socket costs a write and a read system call plus two copies of the data, roughly a few microseconds in all (illustrative). At 100,000 messages a second that is a few tenths of a core; batching 50 messages per call cuts the system calls fifty-fold while the copies stay the same. Measure the message rate before reaching for shared memory.

questions.prompt: A supervisor must hand an already open network connection to a worker process. Which mechanism can do that?

choices.label: A pipe, by writing the descriptor number into it
A shared memory region holding the descriptor number
A local socket, sending the descriptor as ancillary data
An environment variable set before the worker started

questions.explanation: Local sockets can carry open descriptors, and the kernel installs a matching descriptor in the receiver. A descriptor number written to a pipe or shared memory means nothing in another process’s table, and an environment variable set at start cannot carry a connection opened later.

questions.prompt: A log shipper reads from a pipe that an application writes to. The shipper stalls for a minute. What happens to the application?

choices.label: Its writes block once the pipe buffer fills up
Its writes succeed and the kernel spills data to disk
Its writes are dropped silently until the reader returns
It receives an error on the first write after the stall

questions.explanation: A full pipe blocks blocking writers, which is backpressure, and can freeze an application that logs synchronously. The kernel never spills pipe data to disk, nothing is dropped silently, and errors occur only if the reading end is closed, not when it is slow.

questions.prompt: A program writes all of a large input to a child’s input pipe, then reads the child’s output. With small inputs it works; with large ones it hangs. Why?

choices.label: Large inputs exceed the maximum size of a single pipe
The child’s output pipe fills, so neither side can proceed
The kernel reorders large writes, confusing the child
Pipes close after a timeout when the input is large

questions.explanation: Once the output pipe is full the child blocks writing and stops reading, then the parent blocks writing input: a cycle of waits. A pipe streams any amount of data, writes are delivered in order, and pipes have no timeout.

questions.prompt: A video pipeline passes 8 MB decoded frames from a decoder process to an encoder process, 60 times a second, on the same machine. Which mechanism fits?
constraints: About 480 MB a second of frame data

approaches.label: Shared memory ring of frame buffers
approaches.description: Frames are written into shared buffers; only small notices of which buffer is ready are signalled.

approaches.label: A local stream socket
approaches.description: Each frame is written to and read from a socket.

approaches.label: Files in a temporary directory
approaches.description: The decoder writes each frame to a file and the encoder reads it.

rationaleOptions.label: It avoids copying 480 MB a second through the kernel twice
Only a tiny notification crosses the kernel per frame
It needs no synchronisation between the two processes
It protects each process from the other’s memory bugs

questions.explanation: At 480 MB a second, two copies per frame through a socket cost close to a gigabyte a second of memory bandwidth, while shared buffers move only an index. Shared memory still needs synchronisation, to stop the encoder reading a frame mid-write, and it removes isolation rather than adding it.

questions.prompt: A pipe holds 65,536 bytes. A writer sends 512-byte records and the reader has stopped. How many records can be written before the writer blocks?
assumptions: The pipe starts empty
Records are packed with no overhead
questions.explanation: Sanity check: 64 KiB is small, so a stalled reader blocks a busy writer within moments; size the reader for peak rate or put a bounded queue with an explicit drop policy in between.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for one message sent from process A to process B over a local socket.

items.label: B’s read call copies the message into B’s memory
A’s write call copies the message into a kernel buffer
B processes the message
The kernel marks B’s end as readable and wakes B if it is waiting

questions.explanation: Copy in, wake, copy out: two copies and two system calls, which is what shared memory avoids for bulk data.

flashcards.back: A pipe is one-way bytes; a local socket is two-way, can keep message boundaries and can pass descriptors.

flashcards.front: Linux pipe capacity and atomic write size?
flashcards.back: 64 KiB buffer by default; writes up to 4 KiB are not interleaved.
No kernel copies, but you must synchronise and signal readiness yourself.

mechanism.title: How data moves between processes
steps: Processes cannot read each other’s memory, so data passes through something both can reach: a kernel buffer, a file, or pages mapped into both.
For a pipe or local socket, the writer’s system call copies bytes into a kernel buffer; the reader’s call copies them out. A full buffer blocks the writer, an empty one blocks the reader.

Local sockets add features: two directions on one descriptor, message boundaries with datagram or sequenced-packet types, the peer’s user and process IDs, and passing open descriptors between processes.
Shared memory maps one set of physical pages into both address spaces. Writes are visible to the other side directly, with no system call, once memory ordering rules are respected.

Readiness still has to be signalled: a futex or semaphore in the shared region, an event descriptor, or a byte sent over a socket, so most high-speed designs pair shared buffers with a lightweight notification.
Network sockets to localhost work too but pass through the network stack, so local sockets are usually faster for processes on one machine.

useWhen: Use pipes for streaming output from one process to the next.
Use local sockets for request and response traffic and for passing descriptors.
avoidWhen: Avoid shared memory for small, infrequent messages; it adds complexity without much gain.
Avoid writing all input before reading any output when talking to a child through two pipes.

rows: Message boundaries, descriptor passing, peer identity

numbers.title: Is the socket the bottleneck?
assumptions: 200,000 messages a second of 1 KB each; about 2 µs of system call and copy cost per message on each side (illustrative)
steps: Per side: 200,000 × 2 µs = 0.4 core-seconds per second.
Both sides together: 0.8 of a core spent moving messages.
Batching 50 messages per call: 4,000 calls a second; if per-call overhead is 1.5 µs of the 2 µs, cost per side falls to 4,000 × 1.5 µs + 200,000 × 0.5 µs = 0.106 core-seconds.
Both sides together: about 0.2 of a core, a four-fold saving with no change of mechanism.
numbers.result: Batching alone cuts the cost from 0.8 to about 0.2 of a core here, which is usually simpler than moving to shared memory.

india.title: What the manual says about pipe capacity
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The pipe(7) manual page states that since Linux 2.6.11 the pipe capacity is 16 pages, 65,536 bytes on a system with 4,096-byte pages, and that it can be queried and changed per pipe. It explains that a write to a full pipe blocks until enough data has been read, and that POSIX requires writes of fewer than PIPE_BUF bytes to be atomic, so output from several writers is not interleaved; on Linux, PIPE_BUF is 4,096 bytes.

pitfalls.trap: “Shared memory is fastest, so use it.”
pitfalls.say: “For small messages a local socket is simpler; I’d batch first and use shared memory for bulk data.”

pitfalls.trap: “The child process hung for no reason.”
pitfalls.say: “If I write all input before reading output, a full output pipe deadlocks us; I’d read and write concurrently.”

takeaways: Pipes are one-way streams with built-in backpressure.
Local sockets add two-way traffic, message boundaries and descriptor passing.
Shared memory avoids copies but needs your own synchronisation.
Read and write concurrently when talking to a child through two pipes.

interactive.title: Will the pipeline keep up?
interactive.prompt: Process A writes 1 MB a second of records into a pipe; process B reads them but occasionally pauses for 2 seconds to rotate a file.

choices.label: A stalls during each pause once 64 KiB is buffered
choices.feedback: Right: 64 KiB fills in about 65 ms at 1 MB a second, and A then blocks.

choices.label: Nothing is noticed, since the kernel buffers the 2 MB
choices.feedback: The default buffer is 64 KiB, far below 2 MB.

choices.label: Records written during the pause are lost
choices.feedback: Pipes block writers rather than dropping data.

interactive.reveal: If A must not stall, add a bounded in-process queue sized for the longest pause, 2 MB here, or let B rotate files without pausing its reads.

seeAlso.why: Processes are separate address spaces, which is why IPC is needed
Each pipe or socket transfer costs system calls
Mapped files are another way to share pages between processes

title: File Systems: Inodes, Directories and Links
objectives: Explain how inodes, directory entries and data blocks fit together
Use hard and symbolic links correctly, and know why deleting a file may not free space
Spot inode exhaustion and non-atomic moves across file systems

cards.title: A name is not the file
cards.body: On Unix-style file systems, a file’s metadata (owner, permissions, size, timestamps, and where its data blocks are) lives in an inode identified by a number. A directory is a list mapping names to inode numbers. The file’s name is therefore not part of the file: the same inode can be listed under several names, and renaming within one file system just rewrites directory entries.

cards.title: Hard and symbolic links
cards.body: A hard link is another directory entry for the same inode; the inode counts its links, and every name is equally real. Hard links cannot cross file systems because inode numbers are local to one. A symbolic link is a small file containing a path; it can point anywhere, including other file systems, but it breaks if the target is moved or deleted.

cards.title: Trap: deleting a log does not free the disk
cards.body: Deleting a file removes a name and lowers the link count. The data is freed only when the count is zero and no process still has the file open. A service that keeps writing to a log you deleted keeps the space in use, so the disk stays full while directory listings show nothing large. Restart or signal the writer to reopen its file, or truncate the file instead of deleting it.

cards.title: Worked example: running out of inodes
cards.body: A volume created with one inode per 16 KiB (illustrative).
steps: A 1 TiB volume has 1 TiB ÷ 16 KiB = 67,108,864 inodes, fixed when it was created on many file systems
A cache writes 4 KiB files: 67 million of them use only 256 GiB of data
At that point every inode is taken, and creating a file fails with “no space left on device”
Free space still shows about 75% available, which confuses whoever is paged
Check inode use alongside bytes, and store many tiny objects in fewer, larger files

cards.title: Misconception: moving a file is always atomic
cards.body: Within one file system, a rename is atomic: other processes see the old name or the new one, never a half-moved file. Across file systems, a rename fails, and move tools fall back to copying the data and deleting the original. A reader can then see a partially written file, and a crash can leave both copies. Write temporary files in the same directory as their final name.

questions.prompt: Where is a file’s name stored on a Unix-style file system?

choices.label: In the file’s inode, next to its size and owner
In the first data block of the file
In the directory entry that points to the inode
In a global index of names kept by the kernel

questions.explanation: Names live in directories, which map names to inode numbers; the inode has metadata but no name, which is why one inode can have several names. Data blocks hold contents, and there is no global name index; lookups walk directories from the root.

questions.prompt: A disk is 100% full. You delete a 40 GB log file, but free space does not change. What is the most likely reason?

choices.label: The file system frees space only on the next reboot
A running process still has the deleted file open
The file had a symbolic link pointing to it elsewhere
Deleted data stays in a trash folder for 30 days

questions.explanation: Data is freed when the last name and the last open descriptor are gone, so a process holding the log open keeps it alive. Space is freed without a reboot, a symbolic link does not keep its target’s data alive, and the kernel has no trash folder.

questions.prompt: Why can a hard link not point to a file on another file system?

choices.label: Hard links are disabled by default for security reasons
Directory entries can hold only relative paths
Each file system is limited to 65,000 hard links
Inode numbers are meaningful only within one file system

questions.explanation: A hard link is a directory entry holding an inode number, and the same number on another file system refers to an unrelated inode. Hard links are allowed by default, entries hold an inode number rather than a path, and link-count limits do not stop cross-device links.

questions.prompt: Creating files fails with “no space left on device”, yet the disk shows 70% free space. What should you check first?

choices.label: Whether the volume has run out of inodes
Whether the disk hardware is failing
Whether the file names are too long
Whether the page cache has filled memory

questions.explanation: With bytes free, the usual cause is inode exhaustion from many small files. Failing disks give input/output errors, long names give a name-too-long error, and a full page cache is reclaimed rather than causing this error.

questions.prompt: A 2 TiB volume was created with one inode per 16 KiB. About how many million files can it hold?
assumptions: Every file uses one inode
questions.explanation: Sanity check: 134 million 4 KiB files use only 512 GiB, a quarter of the volume, so a store of tiny files hits the inode limit long before the byte limit.

questions.prompt: A service has its log file open. Someone deletes the log to free space. Order what happens until the space is actually released.

items.label: The service keeps writing through its open descriptor, so usage keeps growing
It closes the old descriptor and the kernel frees the old blocks
The name is removed and the link count drops to zero
The service is told to reopen its log path and creates a fresh file

questions.explanation: The name goes first, but the inode lives on while open; only closing the last descriptor frees the blocks.

flashcards.back: Metadata and block locations, but not the name; directories map names to inode numbers.

flashcards.front: When is a deleted file’s space freed?
flashcards.back: When its link count is zero and no process has it open.
A hard link is another name for the inode; a symbolic link stores a path and can dangle.

mechanism.title: How a path becomes data
steps: Opening a path starts at the root directory, or the current directory for a relative path, and looks up each component in turn.
Each directory maps the component name to an inode number; the kernel caches these lookups so repeated opens are cheap.
At the final component, the kernel reads the inode, checks permissions against the caller, and creates an open file description that the process refers to by descriptor.
Reads and writes use the inode’s block map, or extent list, to find data on disk, going through the page cache.
Unlinking removes a directory entry and decrements the inode’s link count; the inode and its blocks are released only when the count is zero and no open descriptions remain.
Renaming within a file system rewrites directory entries in one atomic step; across file systems it fails, and tools emulate it by copying and deleting.

useWhen: Use hard links for cheap snapshots of files that are replaced rather than modified in place.
Use symbolic links for switching between versioned directories, updated by an atomic rename.
avoidWhen: Avoid deleting logs that are still being written; truncate them or have the writer reopen.
Avoid millions of tiny files on volumes with a fixed inode count.

rows: One directory entry, link count down by one
Only at zero links and no open descriptors
New directory entry, link count up by one

numbers.title: Where did the disk go?
assumptions: A 500 GiB volume is full; listing every file adds up to 380 GiB (illustrative)
steps: Unexplained usage: 500 − 380 = 120 GiB.
Listing open files whose names are deleted shows a service holding a 115 GiB rotated log.
The remaining 5 GiB is plausibly reserved blocks and file system metadata.
Having the service reopen its log frees 115 GiB at once, without a restart if it supports a reopen signal.
numbers.result: A 120 GiB gap between listed files and used space is almost always deleted-but-open files; reopening the writer frees the space.

india.title: What the manual says about deleting an open file
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The unlink(2) manual page explains that unlink deletes a name from the file system, and if that name was the last link to a file and no processes have the file open, the file is deleted and its space made available for reuse. If the name was the last link but any processes still have the file open, the file remains in existence until the last file descriptor referring to it is closed. The inode(7) page describes the link count field as the number of hard links to the file.

pitfalls.trap: “I deleted the log but the disk is still full; the disk must be broken.”
pitfalls.say: “A process probably still holds it open; I’d find it and make it reopen its log.”

pitfalls.trap: “Plenty of free space, so file creation can’t fail.”
pitfalls.say: “Inodes can run out first with tiny files; I’d check inode usage too.”

takeaways: Directories map names to inodes; inodes hold everything else.
Space is freed only when no links and no open descriptors remain.
Inodes can run out while bytes are free.
Rename is atomic only within one file system.

interactive.title: What does the reader see?
interactive.prompt: A deploy writes a new 2 GB data file on a scratch disk, then moves it to its final path on a different disk while a service is reading that path.

choices.label: Possibly a partly copied file, since the move is a copy across disks
choices.feedback: Right: across file systems the move copies data, and the reader can open the target mid-copy.

choices.label: Either the old file or the new one, as a move is atomic
choices.feedback: That holds only for a rename within one file system.

choices.label: An error, since moving across disks is not allowed
choices.feedback: The rename call fails, but move tools fall back to copying, so the move succeeds slowly.

interactive.reveal: Write the new file to a temporary name on the destination disk, flush it, then rename it into place; the rename within one file system is atomic.

seeAlso.why: The page cache and fsync behind every file write
Open descriptors keep deleted files alive
A mapped file depends on the inode staying put

title: Namespaces: How Containers Isolate Processes
objectives: Name what each kind of namespace isolates
Explain why a container shares the host kernel and what that means for security
Map user IDs inside a user namespace to IDs on the host

cards.title: Separate views of one kernel
cards.body: A namespace gives a group of processes their own instance of one global resource. Linux has namespaces for process IDs, mount points, networking, hostname, inter-process communication objects, user and group IDs, control group views and clocks. A container is ordinary processes placed in a fresh set of these, plus control groups to limit what they use and dropped privileges to limit what they may do.

cards.title: Worked example: one process, two views
cards.body: What a containerised web server sees, against what the host sees (illustrative IDs).
steps: Inside, it is PID 1; on the host, the same process is PID 48,213
Inside, it has its own loopback and an interface with its own address, so it can bind port 80 even if the host or other containers also use port 80
Inside, the root directory is the image’s file system; the host’s files are not visible unless mounted in
Inside, it runs as user 0; through the user namespace that maps to host user 100,000, an unprivileged account

cards.title: Trap: localhost inside a container is not the host
cards.body: In its own network namespace, a container has its own loopback interface. A service in the container that connects to localhost reaches only the container itself, not a database listening on the host’s loopback; and a server that binds only to the container’s loopback cannot be reached through published ports. Bind servers to all interfaces in the container, and reach the host through an address it exposes.

cards.title: Misconception: a container is a small virtual machine
cards.body: A virtual machine runs its own kernel on emulated hardware; a container’s processes make system calls straight into the host’s kernel. Namespaces change what they can see, not which kernel serves them. A kernel bug, a container given broad privileges, or a host directory mounted inside can let a process affect the host. For untrusted code, add a user namespace, drop privileges, filter system calls, or use a sandbox with its own kernel.

cards.title: Root inside, nobody outside
cards.body: A user namespace maps a range of IDs inside to a range outside: for example, inside IDs 0 to 65,535 become host IDs 100,000 to 165,535. A process that is root inside has full privileges over resources owned by its namespaces, but on the host it is user 100,000, so files and devices it was not given stay out of reach. Without a user namespace, root in a container is host root with some privileges removed.

questions.prompt: Two containers on one host both run a server listening on port 8080. Why do they not conflict?

choices.label: Each container has its own network namespace and ports
The kernel renumbers the second server’s port to 8081
Control groups give each container a share of the port
Only one actually listens; the other waits for it to stop

questions.explanation: Each network namespace has its own interfaces and port space, so the same port can be bound in both. The kernel never renumbers ports, control groups limit resources rather than separating ports, and both servers really do listen.

questions.prompt: Which statement about containers and the host kernel is correct?

choices.label: Each container boots its own copy of the kernel
Containers run on the host kernel through system calls
Containers translate system calls into hypervisor calls
The kernel is copied into the image when it is built

questions.explanation: Container processes are host processes in separate namespaces, so their system calls go to the host kernel. Booting a separate kernel describes a virtual machine, there is no hypervisor translation, and images contain user-space files, not a kernel the container runs.

questions.prompt: An application in a container connects to localhost:5432 to reach a database running on the host’s loopback interface, and the connection is refused. Why?

choices.label: Databases do not accept connections from containers
Port 5432 is reserved inside containers
The connection needs a user namespace to be allowed
Localhost there is the container’s own loopback

questions.explanation: The container’s network namespace has its own loopback, so localhost reaches the container, where nothing listens on 5432. Databases accept any permitted client, no port is reserved inside containers, and user namespaces govern IDs and privileges, not routing.

questions.prompt: A process runs as root inside a container with a user namespace mapping inside ID 0 to host ID 100,000. It writes into a host directory mounted into the container. What can it do there?

choices.label: Whatever host user 100,000 may do with those files
Anything, because it is root inside the container
Nothing, since mounted directories are read-only
Only read files owned by host root

questions.explanation: On the host the process is user 100,000, so ordinary permissions for that account apply. Root inside does not mean root on the host when a user namespace is used, mounts are writable unless made read-only, and reading root-owned files depends on their permissions, not on a special rule.

questions.prompt: A user namespace maps inside IDs 0 to 65,535 to host IDs starting at 100,000. A process runs as user 1,000 inside. What is its host user ID?
assumptions: The mapping is one contiguous range
IDs map in order
questions.explanation: Design implication: give each container a different host range so that two containers’ user 1,000 cannot read each other’s files on a shared volume.

questions.prompt: Order the steps a container runtime takes to start a containerised process.

items.label: Set up its root file system and mounts
Run the image’s program as the process
Create new namespaces for the process
Apply control group limits and drop privileges

questions.explanation: Namespaces first, so the mounts land in the new view; limits and privilege drops before the untrusted program starts.

flashcards.back: Gives a group of processes their own instance of one global resource, such as process IDs or the network stack.
Containers share the host kernel; a virtual machine runs its own.
Maps IDs inside to an unprivileged range on the host, so root inside is not root outside.

mechanism.title: What a runtime builds
steps: The runtime creates a child process with flags requesting new namespaces: process IDs, mounts, network, hostname, inter-process communication, and often user IDs and control group views.
In the new mount namespace it mounts the image’s layers as the root file system, adds special file systems such as the process list, and mounts any volumes requested.
In the new network namespace it creates a virtual interface pair, puts one end inside, and connects the other to a bridge on the host with address translation for published ports.
It places the process in a control group with CPU and memory limits, drops privileges it does not need, and often installs a filter that blocks rarely needed system calls.
Finally it runs the image’s entry program, which becomes PID 1 in the new process ID namespace and must handle signals and reap children.

Every system call the program makes still runs in the host kernel; namespaces only decide which instance of each resource it sees. That is why containers start in milliseconds and share memory for common files, and also why a kernel flaw reachable from inside affects every container on the host.

useWhen: Use user namespaces so root inside a container is unprivileged on the host.
Use separate network namespaces so services can bind standard ports without conflicts.
avoidWhen: Avoid running untrusted code in containers with broad privileges or host mounts.
Avoid assuming localhost inside a container reaches services on the host.

rows: Must reap orphans and handle signals
Host files visible only if mounted
Root inside maps to unprivileged outside

numbers.title: Ranges for many containers
assumptions: Each container gets 65,536 IDs; host IDs 100,000 and up are free for this; IDs are 32-bit (illustrative policy)
steps: Container n starts at 100,000 + n × 65,536.
Container 10 starts at 100,000 + 655,360 = 755,360 and ends at 820,895.
Space available: about 4,294,967,295 − 100,000 ≈ 4.29 billion IDs.
Containers that fit: 4,294,867,295 ÷ 65,536 ≈ 65,534, more than any one host runs.
numbers.result: Giving each container its own 65,536-ID range costs nothing in practice, and keeps containers from sharing host identities.

india.title: What the manual says about privileges inside a user namespace
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The user_namespaces(7) manual page explains that a process created in a new user namespace gains a full set of capabilities in that namespace, but has no capabilities in the parent namespace. Those capabilities apply only to resources governed by namespaces the user namespace owns, so a process can be root for mounting and networking inside its container while remaining an ordinary unprivileged user to the host. The namespaces(7) page lists the eight namespace types and what each isolates.

pitfalls.trap: “It’s in a container, so it can’t touch the host.”
pitfalls.say: “It shares the host kernel; I’d use a user namespace, drop privileges and avoid host mounts.”

pitfalls.trap: “The app can’t reach the database on localhost; the container network is broken.”
pitfalls.say: “Localhost is the container’s own loopback; I’d connect to the host’s exposed address.”

takeaways: Namespaces change what processes see, not which kernel they use.
Containers are namespaces plus control groups plus dropped privileges.
Each network namespace has its own loopback and ports.
User namespaces map root inside to an unprivileged host ID.

interactive.title: Which container is the riskier host neighbour?
interactive.prompt: Container A runs as root with no user namespace and the container runtime’s control socket mounted in. Container B runs as root inside a user namespace mapped to host ID 200,000, with no host mounts.

choices.label: A: the control socket lets it start privileged containers on the host
choices.feedback: Right: control of the runtime is control of the host, and A’s root is host root.

choices.label: B: root inside a user namespace has more powers than plain root
choices.feedback: Its powers apply only within its own namespaces; on the host it is user 200,000.

choices.label: Neither: namespaces isolate both from the host entirely
choices.feedback: Namespaces limit views, not kernel access, and a mounted control socket bypasses them.

interactive.reveal: Treat mounting the runtime’s control socket as giving host root. B’s design, a user namespace and no host mounts, is how to run code you trust less.

seeAlso.why: PID 1 inside a container must handle signals and reap children
Control groups limit what namespaced processes can use
Containers are ordinary processes with a different view

title: Profiling a Running Process: Sampling, Flame Graphs and Off-CPU Time
objectives: Explain how a sampling profiler estimates where CPU time goes
Read a flame graph correctly
Find time spent waiting, which on-CPU profiles cannot show

cards.title: Sampling instead of measuring everything
cards.body: A sampling profiler interrupts each CPU at a fixed rate, often 99 times a second, and records the stack of whatever is running. A function that appears in 10% of samples used about 10% of CPU time. Overhead stays low because nothing is recorded between samples, so it is safe in production, unlike instrumenting every function call, which can distort the program it measures.

cards.title: Reading a flame graph
cards.body: A flame graph merges sampled stacks: each box is a function, its width is the share of samples in which it was on the stack, and boxes above it are what it called. The horizontal order is alphabetical, chosen to merge identical stacks, and does not show time. Look for wide boxes, and especially wide tops of towers, which are where CPU is actually burned.

cards.title: Worked example: from samples to cores
cards.body: A 30 second profile on an 8-CPU host (illustrative).
steps: Sampling at 99 per second on each CPU gives up to 99 × 8 × 30 = 23,760 samples
A compression function appears in 4,752 samples
4,752 ÷ (99 × 30) = 1.6, so it keeps about 1.6 CPUs busy on average
Removing it entirely could free at most those 1.6 cores
A function in only 30 samples has a sampling error near 1 ÷ √30, about 18%, so treat small boxes as rough

cards.title: Trap: the slow request that does not show up
cards.body: An on-CPU profile records only threads that are running. A request that spends 900 ms waiting on a lock, a disk or another service and 10 ms computing appears as a thin sliver, if at all. When latency is high but CPU is low, profile off-CPU time instead: record where threads block and for how long, using scheduler events, and look at those stacks.

cards.title: Misconception: the profile shows what happened in order
cards.body: A flame graph aggregates; it throws away time order, so it cannot show that a pause happened at 3:02 or that one slow request was unusual. Missing names or truncated stacks usually mean the profiler could not walk the stack, because frame pointers were omitted or code was generated at run time without symbol maps. For sequences, use a timeline trace; for stacks, build with frame pointers or provide symbol maps.

questions.prompt: In a flame graph, one function’s box spans 40% of the width at the second level. What does that tell you?

choices.label: It ran during the first 40% of the profiling window
It was on the stack in about 40% of the samples
It was called 40% of the total number of calls
It used 40% of the memory allocated by the program

questions.explanation: Width is the share of samples whose stack contained the function, including time in what it called. Horizontal position is not time, sampling does not count calls, and an on-CPU flame graph says nothing about memory.

questions.prompt: A service’s p99 latency is 2 s while its CPU use is 15%. An on-CPU flame graph looks ordinary. What should you profile next?

choices.label: Instructions per cycle, to look for cache misses
A higher sampling rate on the same CPU profile
Time threads spend blocked, with stacks
Heap allocation counts per function

questions.explanation: Low CPU with high latency means requests mostly wait, and only off-CPU analysis shows where. Cache-miss and finer CPU sampling still look only at running time, and allocation counts measure memory churn, which is unlikely to explain 2 s at 15% CPU.

questions.prompt: Why do many profilers sample at 99 per second rather than 100?

choices.label: To stay below a kernel limit of 100 samples per second
To leave one sample slot for the profiler itself
To avoid lining up with work that runs at round rates
Because sample counts must be odd for the statistics

questions.explanation: Timers and periodic tasks often run at 100 Hz or multiples, and sampling in step with them would over- or under-count them. The kernel allows far higher rates, the profiler does not need a slot, and the statistics do not require odd counts.

questions.prompt: A flame graph shows many stacks ending in boxes labelled only with hexadecimal addresses. What is the likely cause?

choices.label: The program spends that time inside the kernel
The profiler cannot map addresses to function names
Those functions were inlined by the compiler
The samples were taken while the CPU was idle

questions.explanation: Raw addresses mean symbols were missing, as with stripped binaries or code generated at run time without a symbol map. Kernel functions are named when kernel symbols are available, inlined functions vanish into their caller rather than becoming addresses, and idle time shows as an idle stack.

questions.prompt: A profile samples each of 8 CPUs 99 times a second for 30 s. One function appears in 4,752 samples. About how many cores does it keep busy?
assumptions: Samples are spread evenly over time
Each sample represents 1/99 s of one CPU
questions.explanation: Sanity check: the total possible is 8 cores, or 23,760 samples, so this function is 20% of the machine; dividing by all samples instead gives 0.2, a fraction rather than a core count.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of investigating a service whose latency is high but CPU use is low.

items.label: Record where threads block and how long they stay off the CPU
Fix that wait, then re-measure latency
Confirm from metrics that CPU is not saturated
Group the blocked time by stack to find the main wait

questions.explanation: Rule out CPU first, measure waiting with stacks, attribute it, then change one thing and measure again.

flashcards.back: Records the running stack at a fixed rate; sample share approximates CPU share.
Share of samples containing that function; horizontal order is not time.
Measures where and how long threads block, for latency that CPU profiles miss.

mechanism.title: How a sampling profile is built
steps: The profiler asks the kernel for a timer or hardware counter event on each CPU at a chosen rate, such as 99 per second.
At each event the kernel interrupts the running thread and records its instruction address and, if asked, its call stack, walking frame pointers or copying part of the stack to unwind later.
Samples go into a buffer that the profiler drains; afterwards addresses are mapped to function names using symbol tables or maps written by run-time compilers.
Identical stacks are counted. A flame graph draws each stack as a tower of boxes, merging common prefixes, with width proportional to count.
Off-CPU profiling instead records scheduler switch-out and wake-up events with stacks; time between them is attributed to the blocking stack, showing locks, I/O and sleeps.

Accuracy grows with sample count: the relative error of a function’s share is roughly one divided by the square root of its samples. Short bursts of work between samples can be missed or over-counted by chance, so profiles of rare events need longer windows or tracing.

useWhen: Use sampling profiles in production when CPU is high.
Use off-CPU profiles when latency is high but CPU is low.
avoidWhen: Avoid instrumenting every function on hot paths; overhead distorts the result.
Avoid drawing conclusions from boxes with only a few dozen samples.

numbers.title: How long to profile
assumptions: A function is suspected of using about 2% of CPU on a 4-CPU host; you want its share within about ±10% relative error; sampling at 99 per second (illustrative)
steps: Relative error ≈ 1 ÷ √n, so ±10% needs n ≈ 100 samples of that function.
At 2% share, total samples needed: 100 ÷ 0.02 = 5,000.
Samples per second across the host: 99 × 4 = 396.
Duration: 5,000 ÷ 396 ≈ 13 s; profile for 30 s to allow for uneven load.
numbers.result: About 13 seconds of sampling pins down a 2% function to within roughly 10%, which is why 30 to 60 second profiles are a common default.

india.title: What the manual says about sampling options
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The perf-record(1) manual page describes the frequency option as profiling at a chosen frequency, throttled down if it exceeds the kernel’s maximum allowed sample rate, and the -g option as enabling call-graph recording, the stack backtrace, for both kernel space and user space. It lists frame-pointer, debugging-information and branch-record methods for walking the stack, which is why missing frame pointers produce truncated stacks. The perf-sched(1) page covers recording scheduler events, the raw material for off-CPU analysis.

pitfalls.trap: “The flame graph shows the slow part started at the left.”
pitfalls.say: “The x-axis isn’t time; wide boxes are where CPU goes, and for order I’d use a trace.”

pitfalls.trap: “CPU profile looks fine, so the code isn’t slow.”
pitfalls.say: “If latency is high and CPU is low, requests are waiting; I’d profile off-CPU time.”

takeaways: Sampling estimates CPU share with low overhead.
Flame graph width is sample share; horizontal order is not time.
Off-CPU profiling finds waits that CPU profiles miss.
More samples mean smaller error; ignore tiny boxes.

interactive.title: Where will the slow requests show up?
interactive.prompt: Requests take 800 ms: 20 ms of computation and 780 ms waiting for a lock held by a background job. You capture an on-CPU flame graph.

choices.label: Barely: the request path is a thin slice, and the lock wait is absent
choices.feedback: Right: waiting threads are not running, so they are not sampled.

choices.label: As a wide box for the lock function, since that is where time goes
choices.feedback: A sleeping waiter is off the CPU; the lock appears only if waiters spin.

choices.label: As the widest tower, because slow requests dominate the profile
choices.feedback: Width reflects CPU samples, and these requests use little CPU.

interactive.reveal: An off-CPU profile would show the 780 ms under the lock-wait stack, and an on-CPU profile of the background job would show what it does while holding the lock.
